answer: The registration of title to every land parcel under this Act must be “in accordance with the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.” Applied here, the parcel being brought under the title-registration system must have its registration of title follow that cadastral map.

The Commissioner of Title Settlement shall, on receipt of the certified copies of cadastral maps, “publish a Notice in the Gazette, calling for any claimants to the land parcel specified in such Notice to submit their claims to him within a prescribed period from the date of publication of such Notice.” After claims are made in response to that Notice, the Commissioner of Title Settlement shall “cause an investigation to be conducted in order to determine the genuinness or otherwise of claims made in response to a Notice under section 12.”

The provisions create two different routes to the District Court.

1. **Reference of disputed claims during investigation**: If, during the course of investigations, the Commissioner of Title Settlement forms the opinion that, because the claims are disputed, it would be more appropriate for the investigations to be carried out by the District Court, the Commissioner **may refer such claims for investigation and determination** to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land is situate. This is a procedure initiated by the Commissioner in response to the disputed nature of the claims. [21-1998/section-21]

2. **Appeal by an aggrieved claimant**: Any claimant aggrieved by a Declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14 **may prefer an appeal** against that declaration **within the prescribed period** to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land parcel is situate. This is a procedure initiated by the dissatisfied claimant after the declaration is made. [21-1998/section-22]

So, the first is a **Commissioner-initiated reference for investigation and determination because the claims are disputed**; the second is a **claimant-initiated appeal against a declaration, brought within the prescribed period**.

The governing rule is that for land parcels registered under the Registration of Title Act, a person acquiring an interest is not entitled to that title or interest unless it is registered under the Act. Also, an instrument pertaining to land executed in accordance with the Act “shall take effect on registration,” and any transfer or dealing otherwise effected is “void.”

Applied here, Nimal executed an instrument purporting to transfer an interest in a land parcel registered under the Act, but the instrument was not registered. On those facts, the transferee did not acquire the interest, because the interest was not registered and the instrument had not yet taken effect on registration. The private agreement alone is not enough under the quoted provisions.

Under section 48, “Except in accordance with the provisions of this Act, an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under this Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act.” Applied here, the instrument is one conveying a registered land parcel to two purchasers as owners in common. On the stated facts, it is therefore void and it shall not be registered under the Act, unless it is made in accordance with some other provision of the Act. There are no facts showing such compliance.

The statutory rule is that where land is registered under the Registration of Title Act with a “First Class Title of Absolute Ownership,” the “Prescription Ordinance (Chapter 68) shall not apply” to that land or any interest in it, and the “Partition Act shall not apply” to land parcels so registered. Applying that rule here, the parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, so a claim of ownership by prescription cannot be based on the Prescription Ordinance, and the Partition Act does not apply to this parcel.

Rule: Under section 59, a Court may order rectification of the Register where it is satisfied that any registration has been obtained by fraud. But the proviso to section 59 says the Court shall not order rectification of a register so as to affect the title of a registered owner who is in possession and who has acquired the land parcel or interest therein for valuable consideration, unless that owner was a party to the fraud. Under section 60(1)(b), a person suffering loss or damage may be indemnified for “not rectifying the Register in consequence of an order of Court made under section 59,” but section 60(2) denies indemnity to a person who has himself caused, or substantially contributed to, the fraud, or who derives title from such a person.

Application: Here, the registration was obtained by fraud, so section 59 is engaged. However, the present registered owner is in possession, acquired the parcel for valuable consideration, and was not a party to the fraud. On those facts, the Court shall not order rectification so as to affect that owner’s title. As to indemnity, the person who suffered loss because the register was not rectified may claim indemnity under section 60(1)(b) if the loss arose from not rectifying in consequence of a Court order under section 59, and there is no stated fact showing that person is barred by section 60(2).

The governing rule is that, once the Superintendent of Surveys is satisfied that the condominium plan conforms to the Apartment Ownership Law, No. 11 of 1973 and the Registration of Title Act, he must “certify such plan on behalf of the Surveyor-General,” and then: (a) “file the original of the condominium plan after making a suitable reference on the cadastral map used for registration of title”; and (b) “forward the duplicate of the condominium plan and the application of the owner to the appropriate Registrar of Title.” The Registrar of Title must then: (a) “file the duplicate of the condominium plan in the Parcels File”; and (b) “open a new title register in the Register in respect of each condominium parcel shown on the Condominium Plan and make suitable cross references to such register in the register in which the land parcel is registered.”

Applied to the facts, the condominium plan has already been approved as conforming to the applicable laws, so the Superintendent should certify it, file the original with the suitable cadastral-map reference, and send the duplicate and the owner’s application to the appropriate Registrar of Title. The Registrar should file the duplicate in the Parcels File and open a new title register for each condominium parcel, with suitable cross-references in the register for the land parcel.

Rule: If a person dies intestate leaving a spouse, the surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property. Subject to that spouse’s right, the order of inheritance is descendants first, then ascendants, then collaterals. As to descendants, children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent; all the children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes or by representation.

Application: The deceased left a spouse and descendants, so the descendants take after the spouse. The surviving spouse takes one-half of the estate.

The remaining one-half is distributed among the descendants under the rule that the children of the deceased take equally per capita, while the children of a deceased child take by representation. There are two child-branches: (1) the living child, and (2) the predeceased child’s branch represented by the two grandchildren. So the remaining one-half is divided into two equal stirpes:
- Living child: 1/2 of the remaining 1/2 = 1/4 of the whole estate.
- The two grandchildren together take the other 1/2 of the remaining 1/2 = 1/4 of the whole estate, by representation.
- Each grandchild then takes 1/4 ÷ 2 = 1/8 of the whole estate.

So the shares are:
- Surviving spouse: 1/2
- Living child: 1/4
- Each grandchild: 1/8

Under Wills Ordinance s 5, “Every will made beyond the limits of Sri Lanka containing any devise or disposition of immovable property situate within Sri Lanka,” if it “shall have been duly made and executed according to and in conformity with the forms and solemnities prescribed by the law of the country where the same shall have been so made and executed,” and if made by a person who “by the law of such country or of Sri Lanka if competent to make a will,” “shall be valid and effectual to alienate and pass the property” in that immovable property. 

Applied here, the will was executed outside Sri Lanka, disposes of immovable property in Sri Lanka, complies with the formalities of the country of execution, and the testator was competent under that country’s law. On those facts, the foreign will is capable of validly passing the Sri Lankan immovable property.

Before any precept or order for the service of notice or summons is issued in an action for enforcing a right of pre-emption, “proof is furnished to the court of the registration of the proceedings or action as a lis pendens” in accordance with the Registration of Documents Ordinance. Here, because the plaintiff has not yet proved that registration, notice or summons should not yet be issued. [59-1947/section-10]

As to security for bona fides, after the institution of such an action the court may, in its discretion, order the plaintiff to deposit “the purchase amount set out in the notice given under section 5.” [59-1947/section-11]

If the plaintiff defaults in depositing that amount within the period allowed by the court, or within further periods the court may allow, “not exceeding three months in the aggregate,” the plaintiff’s action “shall be struck off the roll of pending cases.” [59-1947/section-11]

The statutory rule is that “A mortgage of a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot shall, if it is effected on or after the appointed day, be null and void notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law.” Here, the owner of a tea estate mortgages a physically divided portion of that estate as a separate lot after the appointed day. That falls within the rule, so the mortgage is null and void.

The rule is that “No share in the common elements of a registered, Condominium Property or of a registered Semi Condominium Property shall be disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of such property,” and “any alienation of any condominium parcel shall be deemed also to convey the undivided share of the owner in the common elements appertaining to that condominium parcel notwithstanding the fact that no specific or particular reference has been made thereto in the instrument or deed relating to such alienation.” [11-1973/section-11]

Applied here, the apartment owner cannot sell the share in the common elements separately while retaining the condominium parcel. If the condominium parcel is transferred, the undivided share in the common elements attached to that parcel is also deemed to be transferred with it, even if the deed does not specifically mention that share. [11-1973/section-11]

The statutory rule is that "The Partition Law shall not apply to any land or building comprised in any registered Condominium Plan." Applied here, the property is land and a building already comprised in a registered Condominium Plan, so the Partition Law does not apply to that property.

Under the Survey Act, a plan or map is receivable in evidence only if it satisfies one of the statutory routes shown in the supplied text: (a) it is made "by or on behalf of the Surveyor-General by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him" and is "certified by the Surveyor-General or by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him for such purpose"; or (b) it is "certified by a registered licensed surveyor". Applied to the background, the land plan may be tendered only if it falls within one of those prescribed preparation-and-certification categories; the facts given do not say whether it does.

A cadastral map, plan, or other plan or map prepared in accordance with any written law that purports to be a true copy and purports to be signed by the Surveyor-General or an officer acting on his behalf “shall be admissible evidence in all cases and for all purposes instead of the original.” It may also be taken as “prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated there in as being that of the original,” and it is not necessary to prove that it was actually signed or authenticated by the Surveyor-General or that it is a true copy, unless evidence to the contrary is first given.

Applied here, the party’s copy purports to be authenticated and signed by the Surveyor-General, so it is admissible in place of the original. Its initial evidential status is prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated in it, until evidence to the contrary is given.

No. Under section 73, “it shall not be lawful for the company to register a transfer of shares ... unless a proper instrument of transfer has been delivered to the company.” So, for a voluntary transfer, the company may not register the transfer if no proper instrument of transfer has been delivered. The exception is that “nothing in this section shall affect any power of the company to register as shareholder ... any person to whom the right of any shares ... has been transmitted by operation of law.”

Under Companies Act, s 79, a certificate “signed under the name of the company by a director and secretary of the company specifying any shares held by any shareholder” “shall be prima facie evidence of the title of the shareholder to the shares.”

Applied here, a share certificate signed in the company’s name by a director and the secretary, and specifying the shares held, has prima facie evidential effect that the recorded shareholder has title to those shares.

The statutory duties breached are:

1. The duty not to act, or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes the company’s articles. A director “shall not act or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes ... the provisions contained in the articles of the company.” [s 188]
2. The duty not to act recklessly or grossly negligently. A director “shall not act in a manner which is reckless or grossly negligent.” [s 189(a)]
3. The duty to exercise the degree of skill and care reasonably expected of a person with the director’s knowledge and experience. A director “shall exercise the degree of skill and care that may reasonably be expected of a person of his knowledge and experience.” [s 189(b)]

Applied to the facts: the director approved conduct that breaches the company’s articles, so the duty in s 188 is breached. The director also carried out the decision recklessly, so the duty in s 189(a) is breached. Because the director did so without exercising the skill and care reasonably expected from a person with that knowledge and experience, the duty in s 189(b) is also breached.

The statutory rule is that “Any alienation of land effected in contravention of the provisions of this Act, shall be void and shall have no effect in law.”

Applied to the facts: because the transfer of land was completed in direct contravention of the Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act, that alienation is void and has no effect in law.
